claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is primarily governed by interface-mediated dislocation pile-up.
Severe lattice distortion in the HEA layers hinders dislocation cross-slip.
Short-range order in the HEA layers hinders dislocation cross-slip.
Hindered cross-slip forces dislocations to accumulate at coherent multilayer interfaces.
Dislocation accumulation at the interfaces generates back-stress.
Interface back-stress promotes localized dislocation climb.
Localized dislocation climb and interface diffusion progressively soften the multilayer structure during creep.
The starting nanoscale multilayer coatings have coherent interfaces between FCC and BCC HEA layers.
The starting HEA layers have significant lattice distortion and established short-range order.
Lattice mismatch and compositional complexity at coherent FCC/BCC interfaces accentuate dislocation pile-up.
Sustained loading will increase dislocation density localized at the multilayer interfaces.
Sustained loading will produce localized deformation bands.
The creep rate will depend on interface coherence.
Coherent-interface samples will exhibit a higher creep rate than disrupted-interface samples.
Compared with conventional metallic multilayers, the HEA multilayers will deform progressively at lower stress thresholds because of their microstructural constraints.
The proposed interface-mediated mechanism dominates when nanoscale layer thickness preserves coherent interfaces.
Increasing layer thickness sufficiently permits bulk-like dislocation motion and may eliminate interface-mediated pile-up as the controlling mechanism.
